Respirometry trials conducted on the Variable skink (Trachylepis varia) at a regulated body temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] revealed a resting metabolic rate of 0.0031 milliliters of oxygen per minute [JOi = 0.0031 milliliters of oxygen per minute], a value that reflects the species' moderate metabolic demands under cool thermal conditions. This measurement, obtained from adults during their inactive phase, is consistent with the reduced energetic requirements observed in many scincid lizards that inhabit seasonal environments. Field surveys tracking recaptured individuals over multiple seasons have provided insights into the species' maximum longevity, with the oldest documented specimen living for 1,460 days [am = 1,460 days] under natural conditions when maintained at an average ambient temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This lifespan estimate, comparable to that reported for the congeneric species Chalcides chalcides, suggests a relatively slow pace of life for a small-bodied skink. The interplay between a low metabolic rate at cooler temperatures and a long potential lifespan indicates that Trachylepis varia may employ an energy-conserving strategy that buffers against unpredictable resource availability.

Neonates of the Variable skink emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs at a modest body mass of approximately 1 gram [Wwb = approximately 1 gram], a value inferred from measurements on the closely related Chalcides chalcides. This low wet weight at birth is characteristic of many oviparous scincids that produce large clutches of small offspring. The incubation period required to reach this hatching stage was documented under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], where the age at birth was determined to be 90 days [ab = 90 days]. This relatively protracted embryonic development is unusual among small skinks, most of which hatch within 60 to 70 days at similar temperatures, and may be linked to the species' reliance on large, yolk-rich eggs that support extended embryogenesis. The delay before emergence likely allows for the development of well-formed, precocial neonates capable of immediate foraging activity upon hatching, thereby reducing early-life mortality risk from starvation.

Reproductive output in the Variable skink is structured around a single annual breeding season, with females producing one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year] under field conditions at an average ambient temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Each litter typically contains 8 young [N_R_i = Each litter typically contains 8 young], a fecundity value that places Trachylepis varia near the upper end of the range documented for African scincids of comparable body size. The combination of a modest litter size with an infrequent breeding schedule yields a relatively low annual reproductive rate, suggesting that females prioritize offspring quality over numerical quantity. This life-history strategy is consistent with the species' occurrence in seasonally arid savanna habitats where food resources for hatchlings are abundant only during brief, unpredictable periods, favoring a conservative allocation of maternal resources. The timing of these litters appears tightly linked to the onset of the wet season, ensuring that neonates emerge during the peak of insect prey availability.

Female Variable skinks attain reproductive maturity following a period of post-hatching growth, with the time from birth to puberty estimated at 365 days [tp = 365 days] when development proceeds at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This relatively rapid sexual maturation, completing within a single year, allows females born early in one breeding season to potentially participate in reproduction the following season. The attainment of puberty coincides with the achievement of near-adult body dimensions, as growing juveniles undergo a phase of accelerated mass gain during their first active season. The ultimate wet weight of adult females, representing the maximum body mass reached after growth has largely ceased, has been recorded at 36.41 grams [Wwi = 36.41 grams] in a well-fed captive cohort. This body size is modest compared to larger members of the genus Trachylepis, such as Trachylepis sulcata, but is consistent with the species' predominantly insectivorous diet and its reliance on crevice-dwelling microhabitats that impose constraints on maximal body dimensions.

Juvenile Trachylepis varia experience a period of rapid somatic development following the resorption of their yolk reserves, with the onset of first exogenous feeding occurring within days of emergence from the egg. The interval between hatching and the achievement of sexual maturation, which spans 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], encompasses a critical phase of foraging skill acquisition and predator avoidance. The species' maximum lifespan of 4 years [am = 4 years], a value estimated from mark-recapture studies and corroborated by captive observations of Chalcides chalcides, is relatively brief for a scincid of its size, yet it exceeds the single-year reproductive window available to many sympatric lizard species at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The interaction between a short lifespan and a delayed age at first reproduction—females typically produce their first litter at approximately one year of age—means that most individuals only experience three or four breeding seasons during their lives, imposing strong selective pressure on per-litter reproductive success and neonatal survival.
